In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the neuroanatomical substrate of reward.
the neuroanatomical substrates and mechanisms of reinforcement and reward in the brain.
the neuroanatomical substrates of motivated behaviors, with particular emphasis on the neural substrates of reward.

self-stimulation is associated with increased metabolic activity in the ventral striatum and decreased metabolic activity in the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala.
there is no evidence to support the hypothesis that there is a specific neural mechanism that is common to all forms of reward.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is a complex organ, and that there is no single region of the brain that can account for all of the brain's functions.

the reward system of the brain, as it has been defined in the literature, is not a single entity but is rather a network of interacting systems, and that the interactions among the various systems are not the same in the case of natural reward as in the case of electrical self-stimulation.
the brain is not a single organ, but a collection of organs that work in concert with each other.
